correctness.rationale: The solution-family equality is a two-direction deterministic proof on the event that every candidate has a singleton-ballot supporter. Every cohesive candidate c must then be elected: its full supporter group contains a voter approving only c. A committee containing every cohesive candidate represents all cohesive groups by a common elected candidate. Probability that a particular private ballot never occurs is (1-q(1-q)^(m-1))^n; union bound yields the family-coupling error without requiring dependence assumptions. Candidate approval counts are mutually independent binomials, so the exact distribution of the proxy solution count follows. The LLN and centered triangular-array CLT establish all asymptotic and conditional claims. An exhaustive exact checker independently inspected 78,664 small full approval profiles and verifies the stated finite proxy; finite tests are not infinite proofs.

originality.rationale: The 2026 SJR/SSJR source defines the exact cohesive-group axioms and empirically studies their feasibility. Its accessible definitions, result sections and experimental discussion contain no law for the entire feasible-committee family in independent Bernoulli voting. The closest probabilistic theory, Han et al. 2025, concerns the distinct all-level average-justified-representation axiom and has a high-density existence-recovery phase incompatible with strong individual/common-winner coverage. The 2021 JR random-profile result treats the weaker existentially covered voter criterion. No accessible identical or stronger theorem was found. Same-model originality, not independent priority certification.
residual_risks: Equivalent independently developed/private-ballot formulas may occur in unindexed preprints or uninspected older appendices; no independent novelty certification.
Only the abstract/secondary citation of the 2017 axiomatic source was inspected directly, though the 2026 full text reproduces formal definitions.

value.rationale: The main SJR/SSJR literature explicitly studies feasibility and the number of cohesive candidates but does not quantify their probabilistic relation. The result supplies an event-by-event characterization of every qualifying committee, a finite-n distribution approximation, the exact feasibility phase boundary and Gaussian-window profile, and a nontrivial conditioning on positive cohesive representation. It gives a mathematically motivated counterpart to empirical feasibility studies, with appropriate fixed-m and iid limitations.
